title: Praggnanandhaa Downs Giri as India Beat Netherlands at Chess Olympiad
excerpt: R Praggnanandhaa declined a draw offer from Anish Giri and ground out his first win in Samarkand as the defending champions beat the Netherlands 3-1 — but India's top-seeded women lost 1.5-2.5 to Poland for the third straight Olympiad.
body:
• Round 5 of the 46th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand saw India beat the Netherlands 3-1 in the open section, with R Praggnanandhaa defeating Dutch No. 1 Anish Giri on top board for his first win of the tournament.
  • World champion D. Gukesh beat Erwin L'Ami in 53 moves for his fourth win in five games, moving to 4.5/5; Arjun Erigaisi and Nihal Sarin drew their games.
  • India's top-seeded women lost 1.5-2.5 to Poland — their third straight Olympiad defeat to Poland after Chennai 2022 and Budapest 2024 — with Vaishali Rameshbabu falling to Aleksandra Maltsevskaya.
  • India share the open-section lead with Germany and Uzbekistan on 10 match points; the men face Uzbekistan in a top-of-table clash in Round 6, while the women take on the USA.

Praggnanandhaa finally converts — and declines Giri's draw

After three rounds of drawing against lower-rated opponents, R Praggnanandhaa chose round five to announce himself at the 46th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand. Playing white in a Ruy Lopez against Dutch No. 1 Anish Giri, the Indian grandmaster ground out a 58-move victory — the headline result of India's 3-1 open-section win over the Netherlands, per Chess.com and The Times of India.

The game was a slow burn that turned sharp in the endgame. Praggnanandhaa willingly damaged his pawn structure to win the exchange — bishop for rook — then backed his technique. Midway through the maneuvering, Giri offered a draw. Pragg said no and converted, a gamble he acknowledged afterwards: "I had to make a call if I should take a draw or go for it. I felt Gukesh was pushing, but it was not really clear to me... I felt keeping the game going can make sense, and it worked out today."

"I had to make a call if I should take a draw or go for it. I felt keeping the game going can make sense, and it worked out today."

— R Praggnanandhaa

The irony wasn't lost on observers: Praggnanandhaa broke his drawing streak by rejecting a draw, on a day when the result he needed was the one he declined to accept.

Gukesh punishes a blunder; the rest hold their ground

On board two, world champion D. Gukesh kept his near-perfect tournament rolling. Playing black in a Sicilian Rossolimo against Erwin L'Ami, Gukesh capitalized on a miscalculation — 23.f4? running into 23...c3! — and converted in 53 moves. It was his fourth win in five games, taking him to 4.5/5 and keeping him among the standout performers in Samarkand.

The lower boards did the holding work. Arjun Erigaisi drew Jorden van Foreest on board three, and Nihal Sarin drew Loek van Wely on board four. No collapses, no heroics — exactly the platform the top boards needed. The 3-1 scoreline flattered nobody and told the story: India won the decisive individual battles, per The Indian Express.

Women fall to Poland again — 1.5-2.5

It was a different story in the women's section, where top-seeded India went down 1.5-2.5 to Poland. The loss continues an unwelcome pattern: it is India's third consecutive Olympiad defeat to Poland, following Chennai 2022 and Budapest 2024, per National Herald.

The decisive result came on Vaishali Rameshbabu's board. Her sister's teammate in defeat, Vaishali — Praggnanandhaa's sibling — lost to Aleksandra Maltsevskaya, who played white in a London System and broke through in 57 moves with active rooks posted on the seventh rank. Koneru Humpy, Divya Deshmukh and Vantika Agrawal all drew their games, leaving India half a point short across four boards that yielded three draws and a loss.

Three-way tie at the top; Uzbekistan next

The open-section standings are crowded. India share the lead with Germany and Uzbekistan, all on 10 match points. Germany earned their share by beating top seeds USA 3-1, while hosts Uzbekistan kept pace with a 4-0 demolition of Hungary.

Round six brings the marquee matchup of the tournament so far: India versus Uzbekistan in a top-of-table clash. A win would give the defending champions — victorious at Budapest 2024 — daylight at the summit. India's women, meanwhile, regroup against the USA after the Poland setback.

The day also carried a quiet diaspora footnote. Anish Giri, the Dutch No. 1 Praggnanandhaa beat on top board, was born in St. Petersburg, Russia, to a Nepali father and a Russian mother before moving to the Netherlands as a child — a cross-border story playing out over 64 squares in Samarkand.
image_caption: R Praggnanandhaa defeated Anish Giri as India beat the Netherlands at the Chess Olympiad.
nri_angle: The Rameshbabu siblings starred for India on opposite ends of a mixed day, and the top-board win came against Dutch No. 1 Anish Giri, born to a Nepali father in Russia.
author: Diaspora Desk
